name: Sauna then cold plunge (contrast)

card.summary: Alternating heat (sauna or hot bath) with a cold plunge to support post-training recovery, so people can train more consistently and build or keep a better physique.
card.aka: Contrast therapy, hot-cold therapy, contrast bath
card.note: Cold exposure carries cardiac and hypothermia risks; cold water right after lifting may blunt muscle growth in some analyses.

quick.overview:
Contrast therapy alternates time in heat, such as a sauna or hot tub, with immersion in cold water. People use it as a recovery routine after hard training, hoping to feel less sore and keep training consistently, which over time supports a better physique.

The usual explanation is that heat and cold make blood vessels dilate and constrict and so help move fluid out of tissues. Reviews of contrast therapy report promising effects on swelling and soreness but variable methods, and evidence is not conclusive.
quick.how: A common pattern is a few minutes of hot exposure followed by a short cold dip, repeated for several rounds and often ending on cold. One example in the literature uses 1 minute of cold at 10 to 15 C followed by 2 minutes at 37 to 40 C, repeated three times. People may do it after training or on rest days.
quick.risks: Cold-water exposure can cause hypothermia, circulatory shock and rarely sudden cardiac events, and a 2024 meta-analysis suggested cold water right after resistance training may blunt muscle hypertrophy, though study quality was limited. Contrast baths are contraindicated during the acute inflammatory stage after an injury.

lead: Sauna then cold plunge, a form of contrast therapy, alternates heat exposure with cold-water immersion. People use it as a recovery routine, so that reduced soreness and swelling let them train harder and more often, supporting muscle and body-composition goals. [1][2]

The proposed mechanism is that alternating heat and cold dilates and constricts blood vessels, helping lymphatic vessels pump fluid out of tissues; some researchers instead attribute benefits to the hydrostatic pressure of immersion. [2]
Research on contrast therapy is mainly in athletes and exercise-induced muscle damage, with reviews describing promising results for swelling and soreness but varied protocols. [1][3]

chain: Heat and cold alternate in short rounds
Soreness and swelling after training may ease
More consistent training supports muscle and leanness
angle.text: The routine is used to speed recovery between sessions so people can train frequently, which builds a more muscular physique. It does not change appearance directly.

paras: Contrast bath therapy involves alternating immersion in hot, but not boiling, water and ice-cold water several times. Claimed benefits include reduced swelling and faster recovery from exercise, including lower blood lactate. [2]
The practice is discussed in training and recovery contexts as part of lifting routines. The goal is to recover well enough to maintain training volume, supporting muscle and low body fat. [1]

A 2013 meta-analysis found contrast water therapy better than passive rest after exercise and about equal to cold immersion or active recovery. Another view is that most benefit arises from water pressure, and a systematic review found weak evidence on swelling and movement. [2]
On muscle growth, a 2024 meta-analysis concluded that cold water immediately after resistance training may blunt hypertrophy, with authors noting uncertainty due to study quality. [4]

Medical and scientific communities agree that ice baths can pose serious risks, including hypothermia, circulatory shock and possible sudden cardiac death. [4] Contrast baths are not used in the acute inflammation stage, typically about 72 hours after injury. [2]

A 2025 review of cold, heat and contrast therapies after exercise-induced muscle damage found heat therapy, especially hot water immersion, the most effective for restoring function, and contrast therapy promising for reducing swelling but limited by few studies. [1]
A 2008 systematic review of 12 randomized trials found insufficient evidence that contrast therapy aids sports recovery, citing quantity and quality of trials. [5]

A 2024 randomized trial in combat-sports athletes compared compressive heat, cold and alternating therapy on forearm muscles, and a 2023 trial studied contrast with compression for strength and glycogen after damaging exercise. [6][7]
A 2025 umbrella review examined physical therapies for delayed-onset muscle soreness. [8]
